To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed an approach that allows the delivery of physiologically relevant and near natural sensory feedback to an amputated hand during the decoding of grasping tasks to operate a hand prosththesis.

we show that by stimulating median and ulnar nerves using transversal intrafascicular multichannel electrodes, according to information provided by the hand prosthesis' sensors, physiologically relevant (near natural) sensations can be elicited and delivered in real time to an amputated hand.

we have developed a new strategy to provide near natural sensations to an amputated hand, by exploiting the remnant sensory pathways and by delivering the information through intrafascicular stimulation of the afferents.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of bidirectional neural interfaces for the restoration of hand function in individuals with amputation, with the ultimate goal of providing them with an artificial hand with a close to normal sensory-motor function.
the development of a new generation of bidirectional prosthetic limbs that can be controlled in a more natural way by exploiting the remnant sensory feedback pathways of the amputee.
the development of an artificial hand with a high degree of functionality.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study by Raspopovic et al. provides evidence that the delivery of sensory feedback in real time, using a bidirectional prosthesis, can provide a more natural control for the user.
this is a very promising study that has demonstrated the potential for bidirectional hand prosthetics.

the present work represents a proof of concept that the delivery of physiologically appropriate, near natural, sensory information can be obtained in real time during the decoding of different grasps, allowing an amputee to effectively modulate grasping force and identify the shape and stiffness of three different objects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we developed a new technology that allows the delivery of physiologically relevant sensations through the peripheral nervous system, and that it could be used to restore sensory feedback for amputees.
we have shown that by using a multichannel intrafacicular electrode array, we can provide near-natural sensory feedback to the amputated limb.

we have shown that by stimulating the nerve fascicles of the median and ulna nerves according to the information obtained from artificial sensors of a hand prosththesis, physiologically meaningful sensations can be provided to a human amputee during real time decoding of grasping tasks to move the prosthesis.

it is possible to deliver physiologically appropriate sensory information to an amputated limb by exploiting remnant sensory nerves, thus providing the amputee with a sense of touch.
it is possible to provide natural sensory feedback in a bidirectional hand prothesis.
